Chapter Seven: Tools and Techniques for Everyday Forecasting
You know, we often think of superforecasting as something reserved for high-stakes situations—like predicting election results or the stock market. But, honestly, these same skills are just as powerful when it comes to everyday decisions. Whether you’re thinking about switching careers, planning a big project, or deciding if you should make a major purchase, these techniques can really help.
So, where do you start? Well, the first thing is to get super clear on the question you’re asking. Vague questions usually lead to vague answers. Instead of wondering, “Will this investment do well?”, try asking, “What’s the probability that this investment will outperform the market over the next twelve months?” See the difference? Being specific gives you a much better foundation.
Once your question is nailed down, there are a few tools you can use to boost your forecasting game:
First up, Base Rate Analysis. Before you dive into the details, ask yourself, “How often does this kind of thing happen, generally speaking?” It’s a great way to keep yourself grounded—and to check any wishful thinking at the door.
Next, try Decomposition. That’s just a fancy way of saying, break the problem into smaller parts. For example, if you’re considering a job change, look at things like the company’s stability, industry trends, and your own skill set. When you break it down, big decisions feel a lot more manageable.
Now, let’s talk about Probability Estimates. Instead of thinking in black and white—like “yes” or “no”—give each possible outcome a percentage chance. This helps you get honest about your uncertainty, and it also makes it easier to adjust as you learn more.
Have you ever tried a Pre-Mortem Analysis? Imagine you made a prediction, but it turned out to be wrong. What could have caused that? This little exercise can reveal risks or blind spots you might otherwise miss.
And finally, don’t forget Regular Updates. Set reminders to come back to your prediction as new information comes in. Adjust your estimates bit by bit, instead of making one big jump. It’s all about staying flexible.
Let’s put this into context with a simple example. Say you’re thinking about moving to a new city for a job. A superforecaster would start by digging into the company’s track record, scoping out the local job market, and weighing personal factors like cost of living. Maybe, after all that, you estimate there’s a sixty percent chance you’ll end up happier in your career—but you also spot some risks, like company instability or the challenge of settling into a new place. As you pick up new information—maybe a friend shares their experience, or the company makes an unexpected announcement—you update your estimate and rethink your plan.
When you apply these tools, you bring real clarity and discipline to your everyday choices. The point isn’t to erase uncertainty. It’s to help you make better decisions, even when the future’s still unknown.
